content: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare inflammatory condition that leads to necrosis of the skin and the formation of deep, painful ulcers. These ulcers most commonly appear on the legs. Initially, the lesions may resemble small insect bites or papules, but they can rapidly progress into larger, more severe ulcers. While the condition is not typically life-threatening, it can result in significant pain, chronic wounds, and permanent scarring. The disease was first described in 1930 and has an estimated prevalence of approximately 1 in 100,000 individuals. Although it can occur at any age, it is most frequently observed in individuals in their 40s and 50s. There are two primary forms of pyoderma gangrenosum. The most common is the ulcerative form, which predominantly affects the legs. The second is an atypical form, which is more superficial and tends to occur on the hands or other areas of the body. Additional subtypes include: Peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum, which accounts for approximately 15% of all cases and occurs around stomas. Bullous pyoderma gangrenosum, characterized by blister-like lesions. Pustular pyoderma gangrenosum, which presents with pustular lesions. Vegetative pyoderma gangrenosum, a less aggressive variant. The exact cause of pyoderma gangrenosum remains unclear, but it is believed to result from dysregulation of the immune system, particularly involving neutrophil dysfunction. More than half of affected individuals have an underlying systemic condition. Commonly associated diseases include inflammatory bowel diseases such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, and hematological disorders such as multiple myeloma. Diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum is primarily clinical, based on the characteristic appearance of the ulcers and the exclusion of other potential causes. A thorough physical examination is essential, particularly of the extremities, where the lesions are most commonly found. Pyoderma gangrenosum is frequently associated with other systemic conditions, including: Inflammatory bowel diseases: Chronic ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Arthritic conditions: Rheumatoid arthritis and seronegative symmetrical polyarthritis. Hematological disorders: Myelocytic leukemia, hairy cell leukemia, myelofibrosis, myeloid metaplasia, and monoclonal gammopathy (IgA). Treatment of pyoderma gangrenosum typically involves a combination of approaches aimed at controlling inflammation, managing pain, and promoting wound healing. Options may include systemic corticosteroids, immunosuppressive agents, and biologic therapies targeting specific components of the immune system. Local wound care is also an essential component of management.
